findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: Capital general reserves fell from £28.07m to £3.49m as major capital schemes deployed.
findings.detail: The authority's capital general reserve was drawn down by £24.58m during 2025-26, falling to £3.49m. Despite receiving £19.00m Investment Fund and £5.78m transfers between reserves, the closing balance represents only 12 percent of the opening position. Capital was deployed to fund £19.73m Brownfield Housing development, £2.00m UKSPF allocation, £2.00m New Programmes Fund, and various other growth and development initiatives. The depleted capital reserve limits future flexibility for capital emergencies or scheme slippage.
findings.matters: A council undertaking major capital programs relies on capital general reserves to manage unforeseen cost pressures, scheme delays, or new priority investments; a reserve reduced to this level signals tightening capital headroom.
findings.figures: Opening 28.07m, closing 3.49m; net drawdown 24.58m; Brownfield Housing 19.73m; Investment Fund receipt 19.00m

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: General revenue reserve improved to £14.09m from £3.88m, strengthening financial resilience buffer.
findings.detail: The council's unallocated general revenue reserve increased by £10.21m during the year. Contributions included £2.00m, £1.00m, and £0.96m from investment income returns; £1.50m capacity uplift; and £0.14m from the final LEP wind-down settlement. This improvement reflects investment returns exceeding budget and one-off grants from closing down the Local Enterprise Partnership. The larger general reserve provides improved headroom for managing budget pressures or unplanned costs.
findings.matters: General reserves represent a council's discretionary financial buffer; improvement in this reserve indicates strengthened resilience, which reduces credit risk from unexpected budget pressures.
findings.figures: Opening 3.88m, closing 14.09m; investment income contributions 3.96m; capacity uplift 1.50m; LEP settlement 0.14m
findings.quote: Approved at Q3 - To: £1m further contribution to reserves from investment income

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: BSIP transportation grant of £12.2m held in reserves - planned bus service improvement spending deferred or reprofiled.
findings.detail: The Transport reserve accumulated £12.2m of Bus Service Improvement Plan funding by year-end 2025-26. This comprises £8.00m from the 25/26 BSIP grant award, £3.30m direct BSIP contribution, and £0.676m legacy BSIP funding received from Nottingham City Council. Additionally, the authority noted £4.00m for 'transition soft landing' was 'no longer required for 25/26' and was added to Transport reserves. The accumulation of this BSIP grant in reserves suggests planned bus improvement projects have been reprofiled into future years.
findings.matters: BSIP is ring-fenced government grant for bus service improvement with expected deployment timeframes; a lender would monitor whether accumulated unspent balances indicate delivery capacity constraints, scheme changes, or grant clawback risk if not deployed as planned.
findings.figures: BSIP in Transport reserve 12.2m total; 8.00m from 25/26 grant; 3.30m BSIP contribution; 0.676m legacy BSIP; transition soft landing 4.00m
findings.quote: This reserve includes a total of £12.2m relating to the BSIP Grant (incl legacy BSIP)

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: Revenue reserves increased to £52.98m from £27.33m - growth driven by new earmarked reserves for grant-funded programs.
findings.detail: Combined revenue reserves nearly doubled during 2025-26, with gross contributions to reserves of £31.86m and contributions from reserves of £6.21m. Growth was distributed across multiple new and existing earmarked reserves including Transport (£19.15m), New Programme Fund (£4.51m), and various new grant-specific reserves. The increase reflects both grants received in-year that are being held for future deployment and accumulation of unspent grant balances carried forward from prior years.
findings.matters: Finance directors monitor whether reserve growth represents true discretionary buffer or tied-up grant balances that cannot be deployed flexibly; a lender assesses sustainability of the reserve position and availability of funds for unplanned needs.
findings.figures: Opening 27.33m, closing 52.98m; growth of 25.65m; contributions to 31.86m, contributions from 6.21m
findings.quote: Total Revenue Reserves  (27.33) 0.00  (31.86) 6.21  (52.98)

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: Transport and highways programmes fully delivered, with £164.65m of £164.66m transport budget spent
findings.detail: Highways Maintenance Block (£75.73m of £75.74m), Integrated Transport Block (£12.86m), Bus Service Improvement Plan (£21.06m), and City Region Sustainable Transport Scheme (£55.00m) are all fully or nearly fully delivered. Combined actual spend of £164.65m against combined budget of £164.66m provides marked contrast to investment and housing programme underspends.
findings.matters: On-schedule delivery of large-scale transport programmes demonstrates project execution and operational delivery capability at scale, providing assurance on management competence even as significant delivery challenges persist in other programme areas.
findings.figures: Highways Maintenance Block £75.73m of £75.74m; Integrated Transport Block £12.86m fully spent; Bus Service Improvement Plan £21.06m fully spent; City Region Sustainable Transport Scheme £55.00m fully spent
findings.quote: Highways Maintenance Block 75.74 75.74 75.73 (0.01)

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: Brownfield Housing Fund delivers £0.28m of £16.83m revised budget, with £16.55m (98%) underspend
findings.detail: Brownfield Housing Fund shows YTD actuals of only £0.28m against revised budget of £16.83m, with £16.55m (98%) forecast as underspend being reprofiles to 2026-27. This represents near-total non-delivery in the council's brownfield housing programme in the reported period.
findings.matters: Housing delivery is typically a strategic priority. Near-total failure to deliver brownfield housing schemes in-year signals planning delays, partner delays, site acquisition barriers, or market conditions affecting delivery — material to lenders assessing housing delivery capability and risk.
findings.figures: Revised Budget £16.83m (including £3.32m 2024-25 carry-forward), YTD Actuals £0.28m, Forecast Underspend £16.55m, Reprofile £16.55m
findings.quote: Brownfield Housing Fund incl 24/25 reprofile 13.51 16.83 0.28 (16.55)

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: Investment Fund and Investment Zones schemes totalling £40.73m show zero spend and are entirely reprofiles to future years
findings.detail: The 25/26 Investment Fund (£26.52m revised budget) and 25/26 Investment Zones (£14.21m revised budget) show zero YTD actuals. Additionally, a 24/25 Investment Fund scheme (Avenue Southern Access, Derbyshire CC) of £1.00m shows complete underspend. These three schemes total £41.73m of strategic economic development spending delivered at zero rate in-year.
findings.matters: Investment schemes and zones are core growth initiatives. Complete non-delivery through Q4 signals either project delays, funding barriers, or delivery model issues — all material to lenders assessing the authority's economic development execution capability.
findings.figures: Investment Fund 25/26 revised £26.52m, YTD £0, underspend £26.52m; Investment Zones revised £14.21m, YTD £0, underspend £14.21m; Avenue Southern Access revised £1.00m, underspend £1.00m
findings.quote: 25/26 Investment Fund incl 24/25 unallocated 19.00 26.52 0.00 (26.52)

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: Capital programme forecasts £67.03m underspend against revised budget of £260.30m, with £65.01m reprofiles to 2026-27
findings.detail: YTD actuals of £193.27m against revised budget of £260.30m result in forecast underspend of £67.03m (25.7% of budget). Of this, £65.01m is being reprofiles to 2026-27 (£54.02m approved, £11.00m subject to approval), while £2.01m is moved to Capital General Reserves. Carry-forward commitments will substantially crowd the 2026-27 capital programme.
findings.matters: Significant capital underspending and reprofiles indicate either delivery delays or forecasting variance, both creating future-year budget constraints. Finance directors need to understand the causes; lenders need to assess whether this reflects delivery capability issues across the authority.
findings.figures: Revised Budget £260.30m, YTD Actuals £193.27m, Forecast Underspend £67.03m, Reprofile £65.01m, Movement to Reserves £2.01m
findings.quote: Total Gross Expenditure 226.75 260.30 193.27 (67.03)

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Budget Monitoring Report - Provisional Outturn 202526
findings.headline: Brownfield Housing Fund £16.6m reprofiled due to extended due diligence and site mobilisation delays
findings.detail: The Brownfield Housing Fund (one of the largest capital projects) is experiencing delays from two causes: extended due diligence processes before contract execution, and the lag between contract signing and site mobilisation. £16.6m (including £1.6m additional at outturn) has been moved to 2026/27 and beyond. The report frames these as systemic features of delivery timescales rather than one-off slippage.
findings.matters: Brownfield housing delivery is a policy priority for regional economic growth. Repeated delays indicate execution risk that lenders will assess; peers will want to understand whether the issue is market, governance, or capacity.
findings.figures: £16.6m Brownfield Housing Fund reprofiled (including £1.6m additional at outturn)
findings.quote: £16.6m Brownfield Housing due to the extended due diligence process required before contract execution, as well as the time lag between contract signing and site mobilisation, which has delayed the planned spend.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Budget Monitoring Report - Provisional Outturn 202526
findings.headline: Investment Zones capital programme £14.2m reprofiled due to slower than anticipated uptake of funding applications
findings.detail: The Investment Zones programme is experiencing slower-than-expected market take-up. £14.2m has been reprofiled to future years, with the authority liaising with MHCLG on reprofile arrangements. The slower uptake reflects both lower-than-expected applications and challenges with bids meeting eligibility requirements, suggesting market appetite or local project capacity for schemes in these zones may be weaker than anticipated at budget setting.
findings.matters: Regional growth programme performance is watched by peer authorities and lenders. Slower uptake signals either weak market demand or governance/eligibility barriers that may require rethinking.
findings.figures: £14.2m of Investment Zones capital reprofiled to future years
findings.quote: £14.2m Investment Zones, slower than anticipated uptake on funding applications for capital schemes, and the number of bids meeting eligibility requirements. The service area is liaising with MHCLG in relation to a reprofile of funding.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Budget Monitoring Report - Provisional Outturn 202526
findings.headline: Public Transport Contribution ('Transport Levy') of £13.48m established following transfer of functions to EMCCA on 1 February 2026
findings.detail: Public transport functions transferred to EMCCA on 1 February 2026. Constituent authorities (Derby City, Derbyshire County, Nottingham City, Nottinghamshire County) now fund services via a formal levy mechanism. The 2025/26 levy is £13.48m for two months of service (Feb–Mar 2026), split: Derby £0.97m, Derbyshire £6.92m, Nottingham £2.56m, Nottinghamshire £3.03m. This creates a new major recurring funding stream and structural dependence on constituent authority contributions.
findings.matters: This is a new structural funding dependence for a major service. Finance directors at constituent councils must budget for this levy; lenders will assess the authority's ability to deliver services within the levy and the risk if any constituent refuses to pay.
findings.figures: £13.48m total levy for two months (Feb–Mar 2026), split: Derby £0.97m, Derbyshire £6.92m, Nottingham £2.56m, Nottinghamshire £3.03m
findings.quote: The final Levy payment due for the part year 2025/26 is £13.48m and comprises both levy contributions and adjustments for Bus Services Improvement Programme (BSIP) funding in respect of 2025/26 grant allocations.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Budget Monitoring Report - Provisional Outturn 202526
findings.headline: Closing reserves at £90.1m, up from £70.1m opening, driven by interest income and grant-funded reserves
findings.detail: Total reserves increased from £70.1m to £90.1m. Revenue reserves rose to £52.98m; capital reserves to £37.12m. The increase reflects the £4m interest income windfall, grant-funded reserves including £8.1m BSIP and £1.6m Spatial Development Strategies, plus receipt of £10m Team Derby grant in Q4. General reserves stand at £12.3m after planned transfers. The authority notes general reserves are 'considered proportionate, given that there is currently no specific provision for risk held within reserves and due to ongoing inflationary pressures'.
findings.matters: Reserve levels indicate financial resilience and buffer capacity. The increase to £90.1m shows strength, but the authority's note on lack of specific risk provision signals awareness of risks ahead.
findings.figures: Opening total reserves £70.1m, closing £90.1m (£52.98m revenue, £37.12m capital), general reserves £12.3m
findings.quote: The closing revenue reserve balance of £52.98m shown in 5.1, includes general reserves of £14m. Of this £1.8m will be moved to the Organisational Development Reserve (£0.5m), Development Reserve (£0.8m) and Insurance Reserve (£0.5m) in 2026/27... This leaves a balance of £12.3m in general reserves.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Budget Monitoring Report - Provisional Outturn 202526
findings.headline: Revenue underspend of £1.46m achieved, mainly from staffing vacancies and lower agency costs
findings.detail: Net revenue expenditure was £1.46m (7.9% of revised budget) below forecast. The underspend primarily reflects staffing vacancies—agency costs lower than forecast and permanent post start dates pushed back in Legal, Transport Transition, Economy, and Strategy directorates. The full underspend is recommended to be moved to earmarked reserves (£1m to Organisational Development and Capacity, £0.46m to Development reserve).
findings.matters: Underspends from staffing vacancies are common and show budget control, but may reflect recruitment challenges rather than prudent planning. Peers will observe how the authority is managing this.
findings.figures: £1.46m underspend on revised budget of £18.53m (7.9%), driven by £0.6m staff underspend
findings.quote: The 2025/26 provisional outturn expenditure shown in the table in 3.1 is £1.96m below budget and mainly relates to a reduced spend in staffing (arising from to a combination of agency leavers and forecast start dates being later than previously planned for permanent staff).

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Budget Monitoring Report - Provisional Outturn 202526
findings.headline: Start-up in Early-Stage Angel Investment Fund entered administration in March 2026 with £0.2m invested and at risk
findings.detail: One of the start-ups in the Early-Stage Angel Investment Fund—inherited from the LEP transfer and managed by Haatch—entered administration in March 2026. The fund had £0.45m invested across its portfolio; the failed company represents £0.2m of that. The investment has not been written off as 'there remains uncertainty regarding the final recovery position' and discussions are ongoing. No loss has been recognised, pending outcome of recovery efforts.
findings.matters: Inherited or non-core assets are an indicator of management capability and hidden losses. A lender will view this as emerging credit risk; peers will watch how the authority handles inherited LEP assets.
findings.figures: £0.2m investment entered administration, £0.45m total fund invested (investment represents 44% of portfolio)
findings.quote: One of the start-ups invested in at a value of £0.2m, entered administration in March 2026. The investment has not been written off, as there remains uncertainty regarding the final recovery position. Discussions and assessment activities are ongoing, and it is therefore not yet possible to determine whether a loss will be realised.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Budget Monitoring Report - Provisional Outturn 202526
findings.headline: Interest income £7.15m earned, £4m above budget, due to higher cash balances and interest rates
findings.detail: Interest income exceeded budget by £4m, reaching £7.15m in 2025/26, driven by higher cash balances and rates ranging from 1.40% to 7.50% depending on instrument and counterparty. £3m was moved to general reserves in Q2–Q3 forecasts, with a further £1m recommended at outturn. This is a one-off windfall from elevated rates rather than a structural improvement; rates are already falling from these peaks.
findings.matters: Finance directors must distinguish temporary income benefits from structural ones. A windfall of this size cannot underpin recurring spending; peers watching the authority's budget assumptions will want to understand how it is being used.
findings.figures: £7.15m actual interest income, £4m above budget, rates ranged 1.40–7.50%
findings.quote: The following interest was earned on balances, which is an increase of £4m compared to the 25/26 Budget

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Budget Monitoring Report - Provisional Outturn 202526
findings.headline: Capital programme £65m reprofiled to future years, representing 25% of revised budget
findings.detail: The authority spent £193m of its £260.3m revised capital budget in 2025/26, with £65m carried forward to 2026/27 and beyond. The report states the budget 'was primarily set based on funds allocated for the year rather than a detailed assessment of what could realistically be spent in the year'. Major delays include Brownfield Housing Fund (£16.6m), Investment Fund (£26.5m), and Investment Zones (£14.2m). This affects cash planning and indicates a structural gap between allocated funding and delivery capacity.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand delivery capacity against allocated funding; a lender needs to assess the authority's ability to deploy capital efficiently. A peer finance director will want to know if this reflects market conditions, governance, or delivery capability issues.
findings.figures: £193m spent of £260.3m revised budget (74% spend), £65m reprofiled to future years (25% of budget)
findings.quote: This represents a carry forward of £65m into 2026/27 and future years, as the budget was primarily set based on funds allocated for the year rather than a detailed assessment of what could realistically be spent in the year.

findings.paper_title: 10 Appendix B Principal Risk Register July FINAL
findings.headline: Procurement governance weaknesses and commercial supplier failure risks both above appetite thresholds and increasing
findings.detail: Risk register identifies two related commercial risks. Supplier failure risk (POCM01) cites fraud and insolvency among causes; procurement governance risk (POCM02) cites non-compliant activity, poor value for money, and legal challenge. Both residual scores exceed appetite threshold (9) and both are increasing in severity. Legacy procurement arrangements and contract management gaps are cited as drivers.
findings.matters: Supplier insolvency or contract failure can force emergency spending or service disruption; procurement governance failures create value-for-money and compliance risk. Both marked as increasing signals controls may not be keeping pace with organizational complexity.
findings.figures: POCM01 residual 12 vs appetite 9; POCM02 residual 16 vs appetite 9; both direction increasing
findings.quote: Weaknesses in procurement governance, capability or contract management lead to non‑compliant procurement activity, poor value for money, delivery failure by suppliers, or legal challenge

findings.paper_title: 10 Appendix B Principal Risk Register July FINAL
findings.headline: PCC and Fire & Rescue Authority transfer proceeding without confirmed Government funding; residual risk 17 against appetite 13, direction increasing
findings.detail: Risk register identifies transfer of Police and Crime Commissioner and Fire & Rescue Authority statutory responsibilities without confirmed central Government funding. The register explicitly lists funding not forthcoming from government as a risk cause. The transfer carries governance, operational, reputational, legal and financial exposure. Residual risk score (17) exceeds appetite threshold (13) with direction increasing.
findings.matters: An unfunded or under-funded statutory transfer creates structural financial pressure; it signals an organization taking on mandatory responsibilities without corresponding funding certainty.
findings.figures: Residual score 17 vs appetite 13; inherent score pre-mitigation 25; direction increasing
findings.quote: Available of funding to finance the transfer not forthcoming from government

findings.paper_title: 10 Appendix B Principal Risk Register July FINAL
findings.headline: Inflation and supplier cost escalation risk at appetite threshold; direction increasing
findings.detail: Risk register identifies inflation higher than forecast, higher energy and operating costs, and supplier/contractor cost increases as risks to service delivery capability. Capital programme cost escalation is also flagged. The residual risk score (13) equals the appetite threshold (13), but direction of travel is marked as increasing.
findings.matters: Cost inflation that outpaces planning assumptions consumes reserves or forces cuts to planned activities; the increasing direction signals that budget assumptions are under pressure.
findings.figures: Residual score 13 (at appetite); inherent score pre-mitigation 25; direction increasing
findings.quote: Greater inflation than assumed reduces our capability to deliver services and realise outcomes, priorities and ambitions, set out in our plans and frameworks.

findings.paper_title: 10 Appendix B Principal Risk Register July FINAL
findings.headline: Transport service cost forecast to exceed levy; residual risk score 21 against appetite threshold 13, direction increasing
findings.detail: The risk register identifies that the gross cost of transport delivery commitment exceeds the transport levy, requiring reserves to be drawn and resources reallocated from other priorities. Rising fuel costs, concessionary fares, and levy affordability are cited as drivers. The residual risk score (21) exceeds the appetite threshold (13) with direction of travel increasing.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to fund ongoing services signals whether a function is financially sustainable within its funding envelope; lenders track reserve consumption as a core vulnerability indicator.
findings.figures: Residual score 21 vs appetite 13; direction increasing
findings.quote: The gross cost of our transport delivery commitment exceeds the transport levy requiring us to draw resource away from reserves and activities that progress other outcomes, priorities and ambitions, set out in our plans and frameworks.

findings.paper_title: 09 Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal audit function's own improvement plan shows multiple delays due to work pressures
findings.detail: The internal audit service's Quality Assurance & Improvement Plan (QAIP) shows multiple actions delayed due to 'time and work pressures': Training & Development Plan delayed from March 2026 to November 2026; Data Analytics Strategy delayed from December 2025 to August 2026; GIAS conformance assessment delayed from March 2026 to October 2026. The report states these will not commence until later dates 'given the high priority work that CMAP Management currently are involved in'.
findings.matters: Slippage in the audit function's own improvement activities may indicate resource constraints that could affect audit plan delivery, coverage adequacy or timeliness of audit reporting to the committee.
findings.figures: Training & Development: revised to 30/11/2026; Data Analytics Strategy: revised to 31/08/2026; GIAS conformance: revised to 31/10/2026
findings.quote: Time and work pressures have meant that this has been delayed further and will not commence until September 2026 given the high priority work that CMAP Management currently are involved in.

findings.paper_title: 09 Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Performance management framework absent in prior years; established March 2026 but not yet audited
findings.detail: Audit identified that the authority had no documented performance management framework during previous years, limiting its ability to evaluate and report on service efficiency, effectiveness and improvements. During 2025-26, EMCCA appointed a corporate Head of Performance Management & Risk and created a Performance Management Framework dated March 2026, with formalized reporting to a newly established Performance Board. These controls are not yet audited; a Data Quality & Performance Management audit is scheduled for Quarter 3 of 2026-27.
findings.matters: The complete absence of a documented performance management framework for a full year of operations is a governance gap that makes it impossible to assess service performance objectively; the recent creation of both the framework and the oversight role suggests this was a previously unaddressed area.
findings.figures: Performance Management Framework established March 2026; new Head of Performance Management & Risk appointed; audit scheduled Q3 2026-27
findings.quote: It was highlighted that the authority did not have a documented performance management framework for previous years, which was viewed to be a weakness in determining the approach to managing service performance and how the authority evaluated and reported efficiency, effectiveness and service improvements.

findings.paper_title: 09 Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: CCTV and physical access controls contain moderate risk gaps; keycard access not managed; monitoring informal
findings.detail: IT Health Check audit identified four moderate risk findings: keycard access to off-site CCTV control room was excessive and included confirmed staff leavers; physical key issuance logs and entry records for storage rooms not maintained; access-log monitoring was informal and inconsistently evidenced; staff screens visible to public areas due to missing blinds and privacy film. All four recommendations are scheduled for implementation by 1 October 2026. EMCCA will share findings with Chesterfield Council and address weaknesses when implementing CCTV controls at its Mid-Term Location.
findings.matters: Gaps in physical and logical access controls create direct risk of unauthorized access to sensitive data and critical infrastructure; informal monitoring procedures fail to provide reliable assurance that access exceptions are identified and escalated.
findings.figures: 4 moderate risk recommendations from IT Health Check; implementation deadline: 01/10/2026
findings.quote: Access to the off-site CCTV control room and off-site/on-site CCTV storage rooms was not tightly controlled. Keycard access rights to the control room were excessive and included confirmed leavers, while physical key issuance logs and entry records for the storage rooms were not maintained.

findings.paper_title: 09 Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: IT systems dependency on constituent councils; cyber security concerns raised and now flagged for active management
findings.detail: EMCCA continues to operate using IT systems belonging to constituent councils rather than its own systems, creating reliance on third-party control assurances. The Audit & Governance Committee raised cyber security concerns at its April 2026 meeting and requested additional assurance. The Director of Digital subsequently provided a paper confirming cyber risks are being actively managed with clear accountability arrangements and defined recovery objectives.
findings.matters: Shared IT infrastructure with constituent councils creates control dependencies and security risks outside EMCCA's direct control; cyber concerns require demonstrable management given the authority's multi-council structure and data responsibilities.
findings.figures: Cyber security concerns raised April 2026; assurance paper tabled to subsequent committee meeting
findings.quote: IT Systems in use during 2025-26 continued to be those belonging to constituent Councils, we have therefore had to rely on third party control assurances in this area. Concerns were raised at the April 2026 Audit & Governance Committee, and a request was made for additional assurance to be sought on the matter of cyber security.

findings.paper_title: 09 Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Risk management framework scoring mechanisms inconsistent; moderate risk recommendation pushed back to October 2026
findings.detail: Audit found risk scoring mechanisms inconsistent across risk management documentation, limiting the authority's ability to reliably escalate and manage risks. Original action date of 31 March 2026 has been revised to 31 October 2026. Management's response indicates this is dependent on building dedicated capacity for risk management, proposing a new Performance and Risk Management function and Risk Management Advisory Group within the Resources Directorate.
findings.matters: Inconsistent risk scoring undermines the reliability of risk registers and risk reporting to senior management and the audit committee, creating blind spots for major organizational risks.
findings.figures: Original action date: 31/03/2026, revised to 31/10/2026; recommendation status: Delayed Future Action
findings.quote: The risk scoring mechanisms are inconsistent across the risk management documentation. We recommend that the scoring guidance is reviewed for consistency across all risk management documents to ensure correct management and escalation of risk.

findings.paper_title: 09 Appendix A Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal audit conclusion: Reasonable Assurance, identifying scope for improvement in governance and control framework
findings.detail: The Chief Audit Executive gives Reasonable Assurance over the adequacy and effectiveness of governance, risk management and control, but notes the framework is 'generally adequate and effective, although some improvements are required'. Seven moderate risk recommendations were made during 2025-26, with control weaknesses identified across governance, risk management and IT security. The authority's organisational structure is described as 'settling down' with permanent appointments to Executive Director roles but lower-level structures continuing to develop.
findings.matters: The assurance rating directly affects audit risk assessment and the control environment strength; Reasonable Assurance (rather than Substantial) indicates identifiable control gaps despite the authority now having stable senior leadership.
findings.figures: Reasonable Assurance rating; 7 moderate risk recommendations; permanent appointments to all Executive Director and Directorial roles
findings.quote: Based on the internal audit work undertaken during 2025-26, Reasonable Assurance can be given that the East Midlands Combined County Authority's framework of governance, risk management and internal control are generally adequate and effective in supporting the delivery of the organisation's objectives. Our internal audit work has identified scope for improvement within the governance and risk frameworks and the control environment.

findings.paper_title: 07 Appendix B 2025-26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: External audit expected to conclude ahead of statutory backstop date of 31 January 2027
findings.detail: Due to critical national delays in local audit completion, Government has implemented backstop dates. For EMCCA's 2025-26 accounts, this date is 31 January 2027. The paper confirms there is nothing currently to suggest that Forvis Mazars will not be able to conclude the audit in advance of this deadline, indicating audit is on track despite the national backlog.
findings.matters: Timely completion of external audit and account sign-off is critical for debt-service certainty; delays can indicate underlying issues or inadequate financial systems.
findings.figures: 2025-26 accounts audit statutory backstop date: 31 January 2027
findings.quote: There is nothing currently to suggest that Mazars won't be able to conclude the audit of EMCCA's 2025-26 accounts in advance of this backstop date

findings.paper_title: 07 Appendix B 2025-26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Risk Management Framework audit identified recommendations with implementation date of 31 October 2026
findings.detail: The Risk Management Framework audit determined a reasonable assurance rating with three moderate risk and three low risk recommendations. Management agreed to implement these remedial actions, but the statement notes implementation remains ongoing with all three moderate risk issues carrying an expected implementation date of 31 October 2026.
findings.matters: The Risk Management Framework underpins how the authority identifies and manages material risks; delayed implementation means the updated approach may not be fully embedded until Q3 2026-27.
findings.figures: Three moderate risk and three low risk recommendations from Risk Management Framework audit; expected implementation 31 October 2026
findings.quote: An internal audit of the Risk Management Framework determined an overall assurance rating of Reasonable, with three moderate risk recommendations and three low risk recommendations, for which management have agreed to implement remedial actions. The implementation of these recommendations remains ongoing, details of the three Moderate Risk issues have been covered in the Key Recommendations Arising from Audits section in this report, all have an expected implementation date of 31st October 2026

findings.paper_title: 07 Appendix B 2025-26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Performance management framework was absent in prior years and has now been established
findings.detail: Internal audit identified it as a weakness that the authority lacked a documented performance management framework for prior years, limiting ability to determine service performance approach and evaluate efficiency and effectiveness. During 2025-26 the authority appointed a corporate Head of Performance Management & Risk and created a single Performance Management Framework dated March 2026 with formalized reporting to a Performance Board. Formal audit of these new systems is scheduled for Q3 2026-27.
findings.matters: The ability to measure and report performance against objectives and monitor service efficiency is fundamental to demonstrating value for money from £38m annual investment power; the prior absence of documented frameworks represented a governance gap.
findings.figures: Performance Management Framework established March 2026; Data Quality & Performance Management audit scheduled Q3 2026-27
findings.quote: It was highlighted that the authority did not have a documented performance management framework for previous years, which was viewed to be a weakness in determining the approach to managing service performance and how the authority evaluated and reported efficiency, effectiveness and service improvements.

findings.paper_title: 07 Appendix B 2025-26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Cybersecurity incident risk score increased to 17 during the year
findings.detail: The corporate risk score for a cybersecurity incident rose and is now marked as increased in the year-end position. The risk reflects potential loss of key information or denial of access to critical systems. The Authority continues to take steps to reduce likelihood and impact, and this risk will remain in the updated Principal Risk Register being implemented in September 2026.
findings.matters: Rising cybersecurity risk in an authority that currently relies on constituent councils' IT systems and is expanding digital delivery operations signals an emerging vulnerability that could disrupt service delivery.
findings.figures: Cybersecurity incident risk score: 17 (marked as increase); risk appetite: 9
findings.quote: 17 (increase) Appetite: 9 EMCCA suffers a cybersecurity incident that results in either the loss of key information or which denies access to critical systems for a period of time

findings.paper_title: 07 Appendix B 2025-26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: IT Health Check audit remedial actions remain unimplemented past original target dates
findings.detail: The IT Health Check audit identified three moderate risk recommendations and four low risk recommendations. Whilst one has been addressed, the statement explicitly notes the remaining issues have not yet reached their original expected date of implementation, indicating delays in closing identified control gaps.
findings.matters: Unimplemented control recommendations indicate identified weaknesses persisting in the operating environment; delays suggest either resource constraints or prioritization issues.
findings.figures: Three moderate risk recommendations and four low risk recommendations from IT Health Check audit
findings.quote: While one recommendation has been addressed, the remaining issues have not yet reached their original expected date of implementation, details of the three Moderate Risk issues are recounted in the Key Recommendations Arising from Audits section of this report.

findings.paper_title: 07 Appendix B 2025-26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Internal audit gave reasonable assurance on governance, risk management and internal control
findings.detail: The Chief Internal Auditor's opinion on the adequacy and effectiveness of EMCCA's framework concluded with reasonable assurance. The opinion notes that governance, risk management and internal control are generally adequate and effective, with identified areas for improvement where management has taken appropriate action. The organisation's structure has now settled with permanent appointments to all Executive Director and Directorial roles.
findings.matters: Reasonable assurance is the baseline expectation for internal controls; the transition to permanent staffing and ongoing embedding of frameworks signals organizational maturity as a two-year-old body moves past its formation phase.
findings.figures: 11 corporate risks closed or managed within appetite over the year
findings.quote: Based on the internal audit work undertaken during 2025-26, Reasonable Assurance can be given that the East Midlands Combined County Authority's framework of governance, risk management and internal control are generally adequate and effective in supporting the delivery of the organisation's objectives.

findings.headline: Authority lacked approved performance management framework in 2024/25, identified as audit weakness; framework approval in progress by April 2026
findings.detail: During 2024/25, the Authority lacked an approved performance management framework and auditors identified this as a significant weakness in governance arrangements affecting the Authority's ability to monitor service delivery and identify improvements. The Authority undertook some performance management activities (delivery plans, RAG dashboards, monthly updates to Senior Leadership Team) but could not evidence these as adequate without a formal approved framework. By April 2026, auditors' planning discussions indicated the Authority had approved a performance management framework, which will be reviewed during the 2025/26 audit.
findings.matters: Governance weaknesses in performance monitoring and how a council addresses them matter to lenders assessing financial risk and to peer councils benchmarking governance responses.
findings.quote: The Authority did not have an approved performance management framework that outlines its processes, expected outputs, and mechanisms for monitoring performance and programme delivery, or for identifying opportunities for Improvement .

findings.headline: Auditors issued unmodified opinion on 2024/25 financial statements, meeting statutory deadline
findings.detail: The Authority's 2024/25 financial statements received an unmodified (clean) audit opinion and were published on 27 February 2026, meeting the statutory deadline. This represents recovery from the previous year's backstop breach.
findings.matters: A clean audit opinion on 2024/25 demonstrates the council has resolved the procedural failures of the previous year and is meeting its audit deadlines, important to lenders assessing governance capability.
findings.figures: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: We issued an unmodified opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements. The Authority published its audited financial statementson 27 February 2026, meeting the statutory deadline.

findings.headline: Auditors issued disclaimer of opinion on 2023/24 financial statements because they were published after the backstop date
findings.detail: The Authority's draft 2023/24 financial statements were published after the statutory backstop date, preventing auditors from completing required audit procedures before the deadline. This resulted in a disclaimer of opinion issued on 27 February 2026, meaning no assurance could be provided on those financial statements.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion indicates the council's financial statements could not be audited to completion, a significant concern for lenders assessing financial accountability and for peer councils monitoring governance.
findings.figures: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: We issued an audit report for 2023/24 which included a disclaimer of opinion. This means our audit report did not express an opinion on the financial statements and no assurance was provided. This was because the draft financial statements were published after the backstop date so it was not possible to carry out the required audit procedures before the deadline.

findings.headline: Bank Rate forecast to fall from 3.75% to 3.25% in Q4 2026; PWLB 5-year rates expected to decline from 4.81% to 4.10%
findings.detail: Treasury advisors MUFG forecast Bank Rate cuts in Q2 2026 (to 3.50%) and Q4 2026 (to 3.25%). PWLB certainty rates are forecast to decline over two years: 5-year from 4.81% to 4.10%, 10-year from 5.39% to 4.70%, 25-year from 6.01% to 5.30%. Forecasts carry significant risk warnings regarding UK fiscal position, labour market developments, geopolitical factors including Middle East conflict, and domestic political events (local elections May 2026, US elections November 2026).
findings.matters: Falling interest rates will reduce the authority's investment returns (currently 3.40% for 2026/27). Conversely, lower borrowing rates reduce future costs if the authority must borrow. The multiplicity of downside risks to the forecast means the authority may need to adapt its treasury strategy if economic conditions change.
findings.figures: Bank Rate current 3.75% (18 December 2025), forecast 3.50% (Q2 2026), 3.25% (Q4 2026); PWLB 5-year current 4.81%, target 4.10% (end Q4 2027); investment return forecast 2026/27 3.40%, revised down from 3.60%
findings.quote: the MUFG Corporate Markets forecast has been revised to price in a rate cut in Q2 2026 to 3.5%, likely to take place in the wake of a significant fall in the CPI inflation reading from 3% in March to 2% in April

findings.headline: Treasury investments of £174.2m as at 2 January 2026, up from £79.5m a year earlier
findings.detail: Investment balances have more than doubled in one year from £79.5m (31 March 2025) to £174.2m (2 January 2026). Investments are deployed across local authorities (£130m), money market funds (£40.3m), and banks (£3.9m). Expected investment returns are 3.40% in 2026/27. The substantial buildup reflects cash accumulation ahead of the authority's capital spending.
findings.matters: The rapid growth in treasury holdings shows financial resilience to fund planned capital expenditure. The composition reflects the authority's creditworthiness strategy, but the concentration in local authority deposits (75%) is operationally significant—dependence on peer authorities for liquidity. Expected returns of 3.40% contribute to revenue budget, but face downside risk if interest rates fall as forecast.
findings.figures: Total investments £174.2m (2 January 2026) vs £79.5m (31 March 2025); local authorities £130m (75%); money market funds £40.3m (23%); banks £3.9m (2%); expected return 2026/27 3.40%
findings.quote: Local authorities 130,000 75%, Money Market Funds 40,300 23%, Total treasury investments 174,238 100%

findings.headline: Capital program of £289.61m in 2026/27 entirely financed from capital grants and reserves with zero external borrowing
findings.detail: EMCCA plans capital expenditure of £289.61m in 2026/27 (rising to £443.31m by 2030/31) financed entirely from capital grants (£284.41m, 98%) and reserves (£5.20m, 2%). The authority has no external debt and projects no borrowing need for the entire four-year planning period.
findings.matters: Most councils finance capital programs with borrowing; EMCCA's zero-borrowing position demonstrates strong financial standing with no debt service burden. However, the 98% grant dependency means capital delivery is entirely contingent on continuing external funding—any reduction in grants would require either capital cuts, borrowing, or significant reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure 2026/27 £289.61m (rising to £443.31m by 2030/31); capital grants £284.41m (98% of funding); reserves £5.20m (2%); external borrowing £0
findings.quote: The Authority currently has no borrowing and no projection for borrowing for capital financing purposes

findings.headline: Authority identifies current grant-dependent funding model will require careful review if funding method changes
findings.detail: The paper acknowledges that the zero-borrowing, all-grants-funded model is unsustainable long-term. As the authority grows and transitions from commissioning to direct delivery, borrowing assumptions will need review and reflection in Treasury Management Strategy. The authority explicitly flags that current funding policy will require appraisal if the funding method changes.
findings.matters: This signals that borrowing will likely become necessary as the authority expands and grant funding proves insufficient for a capital programme growing to £443.3m by 2030-31. A lender would note this as indication of future credit demand.
findings.figures: Total programme expanding from £289.61m (2026-27) to £443.31m (2030-31)
findings.quote: Because these projects only go ahead if the grant funding is in place this limits risk exposure for EMCCA. This will need careful appraisal should the funding method change in the future.

findings.headline: Authority providing loans and taking share capital positions in businesses unable to access conventional bank finance
findings.detail: The authority makes non-treasury investments including loans to organisations that cannot obtain bank finance and share capital positions in businesses, managed through sector partnerships. These are designed to support workforce development and business continuity in the region. The strategy acknowledges these investments support entities where other investors will not.
findings.matters: Non-treasury investments create credit and equity risk distinct from traditional capital expenditure. Understanding this investment portfolio is material to assessing overall financial stability and potential losses.
findings.figures: Angel Investment Fund £1.20m in 2026-27 capital programme, funded from Non-Treasury Management Reserve
findings.quote: This is to enable growth within the region where other investors would not support.

findings.headline: Transport for City Regions capital expenditure expanding from £47.96m in 2026-27 to £419.99m in 2030-31, funded by £2bn seven-year government settlement
findings.detail: Transport for City Regions represents a ninefold expansion over five years from under £48m to nearly £420m, funded by a £2bn seven-year government settlement. This reflects a transition from commissioning to direct delivery of major transport infrastructure including bus services, community investment and asset resilience.
findings.matters: This marks substantial growth in delivery risk and operational complexity. A lender or peer finance director would need to understand how the authority will manage a capital programme scaling nine times over five years.
findings.figures: Transport for City Regions 2026-27 Final £47.96m; 2030-31 Indicative £419.99m; £2bn seven-year Transport for City Regions (TCR) settlement
findings.quote: The Mayor is bringing together bus travel across the region to provide a seamless service for all users. This will include significant capital investment in transport infrastructure across the region enabled by the £2bn seven-year Transport for City Regions (TCR) settlement

findings.headline: Capital programme of £289.6m in 2026-27 entirely funded from grants with zero net borrowing requirement across all five years to 2030-31
findings.detail: The capital programme is fully financed through grants and identified funding sources with zero net borrowing maintained across the forecast period to 2030-31. The authority's policy is to approve only programmes where grant or other identified funding is already confirmed. This limits risk exposure but creates complete dependence on grant funding continuity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand borrowing capacity and whether funding method changes would force the authority to access credit markets.
findings.figures: Total Gross Expenditure 289.61 (2026-27) with Total Funding 289.61; Net Borrowing Requirement 0 for each year 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.quote: To date all capital expenditure has been financed through grants and no long-term borrowing has been required.

findings.headline: Capital programme underspend of £29.2m on £80.9m budget in 2024/25; auditor assessed as timing-related
findings.detail: In 2024/25, Authority recorded underspend of £29.2m against capital programme budget of £80.9m, representing 36% of budget. Auditor assessed this as timing-related rather than indicative of weakness in capital programme management, reflecting that a newly established authority is ramping up programme delivery activity.
findings.matters: Large capital underspends can signal delayed programme delivery or planning issues. However, timing-related underspends are expected for newly established authorities and do not indicate governance weakness.
findings.figures: Capital budget: £80.9m; underspend: £29.2m (36% of budget)
findings.quote: For 2024/25, there was an underspend of £29.2m on the overall capital programme budget of £80.9m, which is timing related and not indicative of a weakness in managing the capital programme.

findings.headline: Finance team comprised largely of interim employees; three interim Section 73 officers since establishment
findings.detail: Throughout 2023/24 and 2024/25, Authority's finance team relied heavily on interim employees, reflecting high turnover and lack of retained knowledge. Authority has had three interim Section 73 officers (statutory finance officer) since it came into existence on 28 February 2024. Head of Internal Audit noted governance arrangements were 'very much in their infancy' and further work required to fully embed robust frameworks.
findings.matters: High interim staffing and frequent turnover in key finance roles creates continuity risks, knowledge loss, and potentially weaker internal controls over financial management and governance.
findings.figures: Three interim S73 officers since 28 February 2024 establishment
findings.quote: Throughout both 2023/24 and 2024/25 the Authority's finance team has relied heavily on interim employees, for example, there have been 3 interim S73's since the Authority came into existence and high changeover in the finance team, which has been made up of interim employees.

findings.headline: Performance management framework absent during 2024/25; implementation expected by end of 2025/26
findings.detail: Authority identified as having significant weakness in arrangements for improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness due to absence of approved performance management framework during 2024/25. Authority undertook performance monitoring activities including delivery plans, RAG rating dashboards, and monthly programme updates to senior leadership, but without formal approved framework. Authority has appointed dedicated Corporate Performance and Risk Manager and established formal Performance Board chaired by Chief Executive.
findings.matters: Without a formal performance management framework, the authority may struggle to monitor service delivery and programme progress effectively, potentially leading to service quality issues, delays, or missed opportunities for improvement.
findings.figures: Framework implementation expected by end of 2025/26 financial year
findings.quote: During 2024/25 (and up to and including the time of issuing the significant weakness), the Authority did not have an approved performance management framework that outlines its processes, expected outputs, and mechanisms for monitoring performance and programme delivery.

findings.headline: Usable reserves increased to £52.4m at March 2025; planned reduction to £24.991m at March 2026
findings.detail: EMCCA's usable reserves grew from £29.7m at 31 March 2024 to £52.4m at 31 March 2025. Medium-term financial plan shows planned reduction to £24.991m at 31 March 2026 due to utilisation of £4m in earmarked reserves to fund transport transition, digital programme, and additional short-term resource requirements. No funding gaps identified in either period.
findings.matters: Reserve trajectories and planned utilisation are key indicators of financial sustainability and resilience. Lenders monitor whether buffers remain adequate to absorb shocks or service interruptions.
findings.figures: £29.7m (31 March 2024), £52.4m (31 March 2025), £24.991m (31 March 2026 forecast), £4m planned use in 2025/26
findings.quote: Usable reserves were £29.7m at 31 March 2024, which was mainly made up from grant income received for future projects not yet disbursed to third parties. Usable reserves are £52.4m as at 31st March 2025.

findings.headline: 2023/24 accounts published 4 August 2025, 5 months after 28 February 2025 statutory backstop deadline
findings.detail: Authority initially intended to produce accounts for extended period from 28 February 2024 to 31 March 2025, but only discovered in May 2025 that separate accounts were required for each reporting period. Accounts eventually published 4 August 2025. Additionally, notice of electors' rights was not initially published with the financial statements and had to be completed in November 2025. 2024/25 accounts were published 30 June 2025 in line with deadline and with required electors' rights notice.
findings.matters: Meeting statutory reporting deadlines and compliance requirements is fundamental to financial governance and public accountability. Missing deadlines signals governance and process control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Backstop deadline: 28 February 2025; publication: 4 August 2025; electors' rights notice published 6 November 2025
findings.quote: The Authority published its draft 2023/24 statement of accounts on 4 August 2025. This was because the Authority had initially intended to produce 2024/25 financial statements for an extended period, incorporating the period from 28 February 2024 - 31 March 2024.

findings.headline: Disclaimer of opinion issued on 2023/24 accounts; unmodified opinion expected on 2024/25 accounts
findings.detail: Authority's 2023/24 accounts were published after the statutory backstop date, resulting in auditor being unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. Auditor will issue disclaimer of opinion on 2023/24 accounts on 27 February 2026. In contrast, 2024/25 accounts were published on schedule with draft accounts released 30 June 2025, enabling auditor to issue unmodified opinion on 2024/25 accounts.
findings.matters: Audit opinions provide critical assurance to lenders on account accuracy, governance, and financial management. A disclaimed opinion significantly limits assurance; an unmodified opinion in the following year indicates governance improvement.
findings.figures: 2023/24 accounts published 4 August 2025 (after 28 February 2025 backstop); 2024/25 draft accounts published 30 June 2025
findings.quote: We expect to issue an audit report for 2023/24 which includes a disclaimer of opinion. This means our audit report will not express an opinion on the financial statements and no assurance will be provided. We expect to issue an unmodified opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements.

findings.headline: Pension reserve misclassification: £100k net asset initially recorded as liability, corrected before audit sign-off
findings.detail: The actuary report disclosed a net pension asset of £100k. This was originally entered as a net liability on the balance sheet. The correcting journal was processed to reflect the net asset position. This was identified during audit and adjusted by management.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are a material component of authority balance sheets. Reversal of a classification error shows the accounts required amendment, though the error was caught and corrected before audit opinion.
findings.figures: £100k net pension asset (initially recorded as liability)
findings.quote: The actuary report disclosed a net pension asset of 100k. This was originally incorrectly entered as a net liability on the balance sheet.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting: £277k of lease liabilities not recognised, accounting policies not aligned to actual operations
findings.detail: The Authority disclosed in accounting policies that it held no lease arrangements where it acts as a lessee. Audit identified five office room leases falling within IFRS 16 scope. Right-of-use assets and lease liabilities totalling £277k should have been recognised. The authority had set a £5,000 low-value threshold in policies approved by Audit Committee but this was not reflected in the published financial statements. Misstatement reported as unadjusted but immaterial.
findings.matters: Unreported lease liabilities understate an authority's financial obligations. The gap between approved policies and published accounts, and the omission of operational leases despite policy approval, indicates control gaps in financial reporting processes.
findings.figures: £277k in unrecognised right-of-use assets and lease liabilities; 5 leases affected; £5,000 low-value threshold approved but not disclosed
findings.quote: Within its accounting policies, the Authority disclosed that it 'has assessed its lease obligations in accordance with IFRS 16 and has determined that it does not have any lease arrangements where it act as a lessee'. During the audit, it was identified that the Authority leases several office rooms that fall within the scope of IFRS 16.

findings.headline: Prior year statutory reporting deadline failure remedied: 2024/25 accounts to be published ahead of 27 February 2026 backstop date
findings.detail: The Authority failed to meet the 28 February 2025 deadline for publishing 2023/24 accounts, breaching the Accounts and Audit Regulations. The draft 2023/24 accounts were published 4 August 2025 but without the required notice of electors' rights; public inspection began 6 November 2025. For 2024/25, the Authority published draft financial statements in June 2025 ahead of deadline and published the notice of electors' rights alongside them. Auditor is satisfied this weakness relates to 2023/24 only and that the recommendation has been implemented in 2024/25.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance is a baseline requirement. A council that has breached statutory reporting deadlines signals process maturity and control issues; recovery in the following year indicates these have been addressed, but the initial breach is material to governance assessment.
findings.figures: 2023/24 deadline missed: 28 February 2025. 2024/25 deadline: 27 February 2026. Draft accounts published June 2025 (ahead of deadline).
findings.quote: During 2024/25, the Authority published their draft financial statements in June 2025 ahead of the deadline... We are satisfied that this weakness relates to 2023/24 only and that the recommendation has been implemented in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Significant weakness identified: no approved performance management framework during 2024/25
findings.detail: The Authority did not have a formally documented performance management framework outlining processes and mechanisms for monitoring performance and programme delivery. While performance management activities occurred (live delivery plan, status reports, RAG dashboards, monthly updates to Senior Leadership Team), the auditor concluded the absence of an approved framework meant the Authority could not evidence adequacy of arrangements. Authority's response states arrangements have improved significantly in 2025/26 with Priority Boards and a dedicated Corporate Performance and Risk Manager appointed.
findings.matters: Lenders assess governance quality and service delivery risk. A significant weakness in performance monitoring arrangements, even if subsequently remedied, indicates potential gaps in how the Authority oversees delivery of its objectives.
findings.figures: Significant weakness identified for improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness criterion
findings.quote: During 2024/25 (and up to and including the time of issuing the significant weakness), the Authority did not have an approved performance management framework that outlines its processes, expected outputs, and mechanisms for monitoring performance and programme delivery

findings.headline: First full financial statements receive unqualified audit opinion despite transition challenges
findings.detail: The Authority, established February 2024, received an unqualified opinion on its 2024/25 accounts. Draft accounts received 30 June 2025 were of adequate quality with some improvements required; the Authority made several further adjustments after publication. Auditor identified no significant control deficiencies. All audit procedures substantially complete ahead of statutory deadline.
findings.matters: Investors and lenders need reliable financial statements. A new combined authority's first full accounts being unqualified signals effective governance transition despite the process challenges evident in draft quality.
findings.figures: Unqualified opinion; audit substantially complete; materiality set at £1.221m
findings.quote: Our audit procedures are now substantially complete for the year ended 31 March 2025. At the time of preparing this report, there are no significant matters outstanding.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: Capital programme of £290M in 2026-27, rising to over £335M by 2028-29, is fully funded from grants and other income without borrowing.
findings.detail: The five-year capital programme includes profiling of the first five years of the £2bn Transport for City Regions (TCR) funding announced by Government. Over 70% relates to transportation. The programme also includes Local Growth Fund capital. The organisation has decided: 'The Capital Programme is fully funded from grant and other income, without the need for borrowing.'
findings.matters: The substantial scale of capital programme (£290M+) presents no debt service burden or borrowing risk, supporting revenue budget sustainability.
findings.figures: £290M in 2026-27, rising to over £335M by 2028-29, over 70% transport-related, fully grant-funded
findings.quote: The Capital Programme is fully funded from grant and other income, without the need for borrowing.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: Local Growth Fund of £108M over four years (£24M in 2026-27) has been included in the budget but not yet programmed.
findings.detail: The Chancellor announced the Local Growth Fund in the Autumn Budget Statement, allocating £108M to EMCCA over four years. For 2026-27 this comprises £18M revenue and £6M capital. The document states the funding 'has not yet been programmed, and proposals for its use will be presented to Board in due course.'
findings.matters: This is substantial new flexible funding, but allocation timing remains uncertain, indicating forward budget plans are not yet finalized.
findings.figures: £108M over four years, £24M in 2026-27 (£18M revenue, £6M capital), rising to £27M capital by 2029-30
findings.quote: The funding has been included in the budget and MTFP but has not yet been programmed, and proposals for its use will be presented to Board in due course.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: General revenue reserves at £8.4M (3.7% of expenditure) are above peer average but the CFO indicates they should grow, reflecting EMCCA's transition to riskier operational service delivery.
findings.detail: Forecast general revenue reserves at March 2027 are £8.4M (3.7% of gross expenditure), above the average of other MCAs (3.4% at 2024-25). However, planned reserve contributions in 2026-27 have been reduced from 2025-26. The Section 73 Officer states that reserves should grow over the MTFP to reflect the organisation's shift from grant distribution to operational service delivery, which carries higher financial risk.
findings.matters: EMCCA is transforming from a funding authority to an operational service delivery body, materially increasing financial risk. The CFO's position suggests current reserves are at minimum adequacy for this higher-risk model.
findings.figures: General reserves £8.4M (3.7% of gross expenditure), peer average 3.4%, planned contributions reduced from prior year
findings.quote: EMCCA should nevertheless aim to add to the general reserves over the life of the MTFP. This is to recognise its expanding role and responsibilities including in the delivery of operational services which, by their nature, have a higher risk profile than a predominantly funding administration and distribution role that it currently has.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: The 2026-27 transport levy of £55.24M is bridged below baseline cost of £60.72M through one-off use of accumulated reserves transferred from constituent councils.
findings.detail: The actual transport levy payment for 2026-27 is set at £55.24M against a baseline net cost of £60.72M. This £5.48M shortfall is funded by accumulated transport reserves being transferred from constituent councils. The Section 73 Officer explicitly notes these are one-off resources 'to reduce the levy requirement where appropriate to do so.'
findings.matters: The apparent 2026-27 affordability masks underlying cost pressures. Once reserves are consumed, constituent councils face the full baseline cost, making the forward-year pressure more acute.
findings.figures: Baseline cost £60.72M, 2026-27 payment £55.24M, reserve application £5.48M
findings.quote: The actual sum payable by Constituent Councils in 2026-27 is estimated to be £55.2M after the application of accumulated transport reserves being transferred to EMCCA and used to defray the Contribution payable.

findings.committee: East Midlands Combined County Authority Board
findings.headline: Transport levy forecast to rise from 2027-28 as grant funding is fixed in cash while service costs inflate.
findings.detail: The baseline cost of transport services is £60.72M. The Local Authority Bus Grant (£21.85M in 2026-27) is fixed in cash terms for three years, while service costs face inflationary pressure. The Section 73 Officer forecasts this mismatch will create budget pressure for constituent councils from 2027-28 onwards.
findings.matters: Finance directors at constituent councils and lenders to those councils need to anticipate this material forward budget pressure in their medium-term planning.
findings.figures: Baseline net transport levy £60.72M, Bus Grant £21.85M (fixed in cash for three years)
findings.quote: Once these one-off resources are used, the levy payment requirement from 2027-28 and future years is likely to increase to maintain and improve services within the envelope of available resources.

news_drafts.headline: Capital general reserves fell from £28.07m to £3.49m as major capital schemes deployed.
news_drafts.lead: A council undertaking major capital programs relies on capital general reserves to manage unforeseen cost pressures, scheme delays, or new priority investments; a reserve reduced to this level signals tightening capital headroom.

news_drafts.headline: General revenue reserve improved to £14.09m from £3.88m, strengthening financial resilience buffer.
news_drafts.lead: General reserves represent a council's discretionary financial buffer; improvement in this reserve indicates strengthened resilience, which reduces credit risk from unexpected budget pressures.

news_drafts.headline: BSIP transportation grant of £12.2m held in reserves - planned bus service improvement spending deferred or reprofiled.
news_drafts.lead: BSIP is ring-fenced government grant for bus service improvement with expected deployment timeframes; a lender would monitor whether accumulated unspent balances indicate delivery capacity constraints, scheme changes, or grant clawback risk if not deployed…
